text: Janet’s ducks lay sixteen eggs a day. She eats three, bakes with four, and sells the rest for two dollars each. How much does she make?
Easy! Sixteen, minus three, minus four, is nine eggs. Times two. Eighteen dollars!
Right. Now ask a small AI model, answering in a hurry.
Twenty-six dollars?! Where did that even come from?
By the end of this course, that same small model will slow down, write out its working, and get problems like this right far more often.
And here’s the twist. Nobody will show it a single worked example.
It learns the way DeepSeek trained R1. It tries. A program gives it a score. And it does more of whatever scored well.
Hold on. No examples at all? Then how does it ever learn to reason?
That’s what this whole course is about. Today, you’ll meet the team, see the map, and get a before score that you’re going to beat.
Teach a small AI to think. Welcome.
Meet the team. First, this is Tiny.
Aww, hi Tiny!
Tiny is a toy model. It answers sums of two single digits, like three plus four, by picking an answer from zero to eighteen.
So what does it say for three plus four? Eleven. Two. Fifteen!
Right now, it’s guessing at random. One chance in nineteen of being right.
But Tiny is so small that you can watch every number inside it change as it learns, right in your browser. So whenever a new idea shows up, we try it on Tiny first.
And this is Tiny’s big sibling, Qwen. The real model you’ll train.
It’s an open model from Alibaba, with about half a billion adjustable numbers inside. Sounds huge, but the models behind chat assistants are hundreds of times bigger.
Then why not train one of those? Go big!
Because Qwen fits on a free GPU. Experiments take hours, not days. And its maths is shaky, so you’ll really see it improve.
Ha. So it’s small on purpose. I like it.
To know if Qwen is getting better, we need questions with known answers. We use GSM8K: about eight and a half thousand grade-school maths word problems.
Each one comes with a worked solution.
And the final number always sits right at the end, after four hash marks.
Why does that matter so much?
Because a computer can check any answer by itself. Take the model’s last number, compare it with the number after the hashes, done. No human needed.
Oh! So a program can be the teacher.
So here’s a question. When Qwen gets a problem like Janet’s ducks wrong, what’s usually going on?
Pause, and have a guess.
A, surely. It’s a tiny model. It just can’t do arithmetic.
Good guess, but no. It’s B. Most of the time, it can do every single step.
It skips a step, copies a number wrongly, or never says a final answer. What it’s missing is a habit: laying out the steps, and checking them. That habit is what we’ll train.
Here’s the map. Every stop is a short episode, like this one.
First, why thinking out loud helps a model at all. Then, how to grade answers with no teacher.
Next, how a score actually changes a model, and the method behind R1, built step by step on Tiny.

Right after that. Your first real run on a free GPU, then reading the training curves, the famous aha moment, and copying a big model’s thinking into a small one.

A capstone, where you train a reasoning model of your own.

Total cost: zero. My favourite price!
For the labs, it helps to read a short Python loop. For the maths, school averages and percentages are enough.
Then, your very first notebook: hello GPU.
Upload it to Colab, switch the runtime to a T4 GPU, and run the cells from top to bottom.
It checks the GPU, loads Qwen, and asks it twenty maths questions, grading each one by its last number.
So I get a score out of twenty?
Exactly. Write it down. It’s your before photo. Expect a mixed score: measurements of this model land somewhere between a third and a half right.
So, lots of room to grow. Got it.
Quick recap.
We’re teaching a small open model, Qwen, to reason through maths word problems.
GSM8K answers can be checked by a program, so it learns from scores, with no human teacher.
And Tiny, the toy, lets us see every idea first.
One last thing, before you go.
Remember Janet’s ducks? Answering straight away, a small model often blurts out a wrong number. Asked to write its steps first, it gets it right far more often.
But wait. That’s the same model, with the same brain. Why would writing things down make it any smarter?
That has a surprising answer. And it’s exactly where Module two begins.
